verses.note: The first word God speaks to fallen humanity is a question that seeks them out. Before judgment comes a call, and the pattern holds through Scripture to the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10).

God covers the shame they could not adequately cover themselves. Many Christian interpreters have seen in the skins the first death of an animal on humanity's behalf and a hint of sacrifice; the text does not say so, and others read the act simply as God's care for people he is sending into a harsher world. Either way the image of God clothing sinners runs through Scripture (Isaiah 61:10, Galatians 3:27).

The first mention of grace in Scripture comes at the moment of the world's condemnation. The order of verses 8 and 9, favor first and righteousness second, has long been read as showing that Noah's rescue rests on God's grace, though Genesis also insists that grace produced a righteous life.

Noah's whole household is brought in because of his standing before God. Hebrews 11:7 says Noah built the ark for the saving of his household, and the pattern of God's rescue reaching a family through one person recurs throughout Scripture.

The one who is saved does not seal his own safety; God shuts him in. The same act also marks the end of the time for entering. Jesus' parable of the ten virgins ends with the same image, the door shut when the bridegroom has come (Matthew 25:10).

This is the first remnant in Scripture: a small group preserved through judgment to carry God's purposes forward. The prophets develop the idea (Isaiah 10:20-22), and Paul applies it to the people of God saved by grace (Romans 9:27, 11:5).

Righteousness here is a right standing with God received through trust. The verse shows the way of salvation already at work in Genesis, long before the cross makes plain on what basis God can count the ungodly righteous (Romans 4:5, 23-25).

Lot is not rescued because he runs but because he is seized. The verse is one of the Old Testament's plainest pictures of salvation as God's act of mercy on the undeserving, and 2 Peter 2:7-9 draws the lesson that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly.

Lot is saved for Abraham's sake. The verse shows God's mercy reaching one person because of his covenant with another, a pattern the New Testament fulfills when believers are saved for the sake of Christ.
Jacob's survival is a gift, not an achievement. He lives because God chose not to destroy him, which is the logic of every deliverance Scripture calls salvation.

God's rescue here is physical survival through famine, and it is also the preservation of the line through which the promise to Abraham will come. The vocabulary of remnant and survivors will later carry the hope of rescue through judgment and exile.

The first use of ‘redeem’ in Scripture is a man's testimony that God rescued him from every harm. Before it is the language of the exodus (Exodus 6:6) or of the cross, redemption is a personal rescue by a kinsman who takes responsibility for you.

Jacob's only prayer in the poem is for the LORD's deliverance, placed amid predictions of his sons' wars and struggles. The tribes' future rests on the LORD's salvation, not on their lion strength or their cunning.

Salvation in the Old Testament is first concrete rescue from those who oppress. The small scene at the well uses the same word as the great deliverance at the sea, preparing the reader to see that salvation means being brought out from under a hostile power.

The verse defines salvation as God's own act: he comes down, delivers from the hand of the oppressor, and brings his people into a good land. Rescue from and bringing into belong together, and later Scripture holds both when it speaks of redemption.

The verse gives the Bible's basic vocabulary of salvation: God brings out from bondage, delivers from a hostile power, and redeems as next of kin at his own cost. The New Testament uses the same language of redemption for what Christ does (Galatians 4:4-5; 1 Peter 1:18-19).

The house is spared not because of who lives in it but because of what is on its door. The verse makes God's seeing the blood the ground of deliverance, and Israel's part is to trust the promise enough to act on it.

The last word of the chapter belongs to God's act: the LORD brought Israel out. Israel's obedience has been real and repeated, but the chapter ends by naming who did the rescuing, the note on which the Ten Commandments begin (20:2).
The emphatic ‘I have given’ makes atonement something God provides before it is something Israel performs. Sacrifice is not a bribe offered upward but a provision handed down.
Rescue comes before command. The law's meaning is explained by redemption: God freed a people of slaves and gave them a way to live as free people.
Redemption from Egypt is described as God acquiring a people for himself. The language of padah, ransom, becomes the vocabulary for salvation throughout Scripture (Deuteronomy 7:8; Titus 2:14).
The plea asks God to deliver the whole of what the sufferer is, his one life. Rescue in the Psalms is the saving of a life, not merely relief from pain.
Salvation begins with God's word of comfort to a people who have done nothing to earn it. The sentence is over because God declares it over; the exiles' part is to hear.

The verb basar, rendered in Greek by euangelizesthai, gives the New Testament its vocabulary for the gospel. Here the good news is that God himself has come. When Mark opens with the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ and quotes Isaiah 40:3 (Mark 1:1-3), he claims that this announcement has become true in Jesus.

Redemption in Isaiah is God acting as kinsman to buy back his own. That no silver changes hands does not mean the redemption is costless: the chapter moves straight into the Servant who suffers (52:13 to 53:12). Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

Salvation is God's act done in public, before all the nations. The second line of verse 10 is nearly identical to Psalm 98:3. Luke's infancy narrative echoes both halves of these verses: Simeon awaits the consolation of Israel and sees God's salvation prepared before all peoples (Luke 2:25, 2:30-31), and Anna speaks to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:38).
Salvation here is healing and peace, wholeness restored, not merely a verdict. The verse joins the legal (punishment) and the medical (healing) in one sentence.

Israel's return is described as redemption, not escape. God acts as kinsman-redeemer for a people held by a stronger power, the pattern the New Testament uses when it speaks of Christ's giving himself as a ransom (Mark 10:45).

Everything in the new covenant stands on the final ‘for’: I will forgive. The inward law and the universal knowledge of God follow from a relationship God restores by pardon. Jeremiah 50:20 repeats the promise: in those days Israel's iniquity will be sought and not found.

Salvation in this verse is rescue from uncleanness, not only from enemies or exile. Matthew's Gospel says the child will be called Jesus ‘because He will save His people from their sins’ (Matthew 1:21), the same kind of rescue: from the inward captor, not the outward one.
The rescue promised is from sins, not only from enemies. Restoration to the land is not enough; the people must be saved from what brought the exile in the first place.
